reading.passage: {'blocks': [{'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit5.passage.p001', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '[A] The fog still chills the morning air and the cable cars still climb halfway to the stars. Yet on the ground, the Bay area has changed greatly since singer Tony Bennett left his heart here. Silicon Valley and the tech industry have led the region into a period of unprecedented wealth and innovation. But existing political and land limits have caused an alarming housing crisis and astronomical rise in social and economic difference.'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit5.passage.p002', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '[B] While the residents of most cities display pride and support for their home industries, drastic market distortions in the San Francisco Bay Area have created boiling resentment in the region towards the tech industry. A vocal minority is even calling on officials to punish those who are benefitting from the economic and housing boom. If this boom and its consequences are not resolved, a drastic increase in social and economic difference may have a profound impact on the region for generations. A history and analysis of this transformation may hold invaluable insights about the opportunities. Perils of tech cities are currently being cultivated across the US, and indeed around the world.'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit5.passage.p003', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': "[C] According to a recent study, San Francisco ranks first in California for economic difference. The average income of the top 1% of households in the city averages $3.6 million. This is 44 times the average income of those at the bottom, which stands at $81,094. The top 1% of the San Francisco peninsula's share of total income now extends to 30.8% of the region's income. This was a dramatic jump from 1989, where it stood at 15.8%."}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit5.passage.p004', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': "[D] The region's economy has been fundamentally transformed by the technology industry springing from Silicon Valley. Policies pushed by Mayor Ed Lee provided tax breaks for tech companies to set up shop along the city's long-neglected Mid-Market area. The city is now home to Twitter, Uber, Airbnb, Pinterest, Dropbox and others. In short, the Bay Area has become a global magnet for those with specialized skills, which has in turn helped fuel economic enthusiasm, and this economic growth has reduced unemployment to 3.4%, an admirable feat."}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit5.passage.p005', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '[E] In spite of all that, the strength of the recent job growth, combined with policies that have traditionally limited housing development in the city and throughout the peninsula, did not help ease the affordability crisis. In 2015 alone, the Bay Area added 64,000 in jobs. In the same year, only 5,000 new homes were built.'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit5.passage.p006', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '[F] With the average house in the city costing over $1.25 million and average flat prices over $1.11 million, the minimum qualifying income to purchase a house has increased to $254,000. Considering that the average household income in the city currently stands at around $80,000, it is not an exaggeration to say that the dream of home ownership is now beyond the grasp of the vast majority of today’s people who rent.'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit5.passage.p007', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '[G] For generations, the stability and prosperity of the American middle class has been anchored by home ownership. Studies have consistently shown that the value of land has overtaken overall income growth, thus providing a huge advantage to property owners as a vehicle of wealth building. When home prices soar above the reach of most households, the gap between the rich and the poor dramatically increases.'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit5.passage.p008', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '[H] If contributing factors leading to housing becoming less than affordable are not resolved over multiple generations, a small elite will control a vast share of the country’s total wealth. The result? A society where the threat of class warfare would loom large. A society’s level of happiness is tied less to measures of quantitative wealth and more to measures of qualitative wealth. This means that how a person judges their security in comparison to their neighbors’ has more of an impact on their happiness than their objective standard of living. At the same time, when a system no longer provides opportunities for the majority to participate in wealth building, it not only robs those who are excluded from opportunities, but also deprives them of their dignity.'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit5.passage.p009', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '[I] San Francisco and the Bay Area have long been committed to values which embrace inclusion and rejection of mainstream culture. To see these values coming apart so publicly adds insult to injury for a region once defined by its progressive social fabric. In the face of resentment, it is human to want revenge. But deteriorating policies such as heavily taxing technology companies or real estate developers are not likely to shift the balance.'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit5.passage.p010', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '[J] The housing crisis is caused by two primary factors: the growing desirability of the Bay Area as a place to live due to its excellent economy, and our limited housing stock. Although the city is experiencing an unprecedented boom in new housing, more units are sorely needed. Protection policies were originally designed to suppress bad development and boost historic preservation in our urban areas. Now, too many developers are experiencing excessive delays. Meanwhile, there are the land limitations of the Bay Area to consider. The region is surrounded by water and mountains. Local governments need to aid development as well. This means increasing housing density throughout the region and building upwards while streamlining the approval process.'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit5.passage.p011', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '[K] Real estate alone will not solve the problem, of course. Transportation, too, needs to be updated and infrastructure extended to link distant regions to Silicon Valley and the city. We need to build an effective high-speed commuting system linking the high-priced and crowded Bay Area with the low-priced and low-density Central Valley. This would dramatically reduce travel times. And based on the operating speeds of hovering trains used in countries such as Japan or Spain, high-speed rail could shorten the time to travel between San Francisco and California’s capital, Sacramento, or from Stockton to San Jose, to under 30 minutes. This system would bring once distant regions within reasonable commute to heavy job centers. The city also needs to update existing transportation routes combined with smart home-building policies that dramatically increase housing density in areas surrounding high-speed rail stations. By doing so, we will be able to build affordable housing within acceptable commuting distances for a significant bulk of the workforce.'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit5.passage.p012', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '[L] Our threatening housing crisis forces the difficult question of what type of society we would like to be. Will it be one where the elite command the vast bulk of wealth and regional culture is defined by an aggressive business world? We were recently treated to a taste of the latter, when local tech employee Justin Keller wrote an open letter to the city complaining about having to see homeless people on his way to work.'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit5.passage.p013', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': "[M] It doesn't have to be this way. But solutions need to be implemented now, before angry crowds grow from a nuisance to serious concern. It may take less than you might think. And in fact, the solutions to our housing crisis are already fairly clear. We need to increase the density of housing units. We need to use existing technology to shorten travel times and break the land limits. There is a way to solve complex social and economic problems without abandoning social responsibility. This is the Bay Area's opportunity to prove that it can innovate more than just technology."}]}

{'blocks': [{'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit6.passage.p001', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': 'The ability to make inferences from same and different, once thought to be unique to'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit6.passage.p002', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': 'humans, is viewed as a cornerstone of abstract intelligent thought. A new study, however, has'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit6.passage.p003', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
shown that what psychologists call same-different discrimination is present in creatures'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit6.passage.p004', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
generally seen as unintelligent: newborn ducklings (小鸭) .'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit6.passage.p005', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
The study, published Thursday in Science, challenges our idea of what it means to have a'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit6.passage.p006', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
birdbrain, said Edward Wasserman, an experimental psychologist at the University of Iowa who'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit6.passage.p007', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
wrote an independent review of the study.'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit6.passage.p008', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
“In fact, birds are extremely intelligent and our problem pretty much lies in figuring out'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit6.passage.p009', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': "
how to get them to 'talk' to us, or tell us how smart they really are,“ he said."}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit6.passage.p010', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
Antone Martinho and Alex Kacelnik, co-authors of the new paper, devised a clever'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit6.passage.p011', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
experiment to better test bird intelligence.'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit6.passage.p012', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
First, they took 1-day-old ducklings and exposed them to a pair of moving objects. The two'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit6.passage.p013', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
objects were either the same or different in shape or color. Then they exposed each duckling to'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit6.passage.p014', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
two entirely new pairs of moving objects.'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit6.passage.p015', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
The researchers found that about 70% of the ducklings preferred to move toward the pair of'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit6.passage.p016', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
objects that had the same shape or color relationship as the first objects they saw. A duckling'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit6.passage.p017', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
that was first shown two green spheres, in other words, was more likely to move toward a pair'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit6.passage.p018', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
of blue spheres than a mismatched pair of orange and purple spheres.'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit6.passage.p019', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': "
Ducklings go through a rapid learning process called imprinting shortly after birth一it's"}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit6.passage.p020', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
what allows them to identify and follow their mothers.'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit6.passage.p021', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
These findings suggest that ducklings use abstract relationships between sensory inputs like color, shape, sounds and odor to recognize their mothers, said Dr. Kacelnik.'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit6.passage.p022', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
By studying imprinting, the authors of this study have shown for the first time that an'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit6.passage.p023', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
animal can learn relationships between concepts without training, said Jeffrey Katz, an'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit6.passage.p024', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
experimental psychologist at Auburn University who was not involved in the study.'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit6.passage.p025', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
Previous studies have suggested that other animals, including pigeons, dolphins, honeybees'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit6.passage.p026', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
and some primates (灵长类动物)， can discern same from different, but only after extensive'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit6.passage.p027', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
training.'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit6.passage.p028', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
Adding ducklings to the list-particularly untrained newborn ducklings一suggests that the'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit6.passage.p029', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
ability to compare abstract concepts “is far more necessary to a wider variety of animals5'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit6.passage.p030', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
survival than we previously thought, Dr. Martinho said.He believes the ability is so crucial'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit6.passage.p031', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
because it helps animals consider context when identifying objects in their environment.'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit6.passage.p032', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
It's clear from this study and others like it that "animals process and appreciate far more of'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit6.passage.p033', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
the intricacies in their world than we've ever understood, Dr. Wasserman said. "We are in a'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit6.passage.p034', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
revolutionary phase in terms of our ability to understand the minds of other animals.^^'}]}

{'blocks': [{'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit7.passage.p001', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': 'The suggestion that people should aim for dietary diversity by trying to eat a variety of'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit7.passage.p002', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': 'foods has been a basic public health recommendation for decades in the United States and'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit7.passage.p003', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
elsewhere. Now, however, experts are warning that aiming for a diverse diet may actually lead'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit7.passage.p004', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
to just eating more calories, and, thus, to obesity. One issue is that people may not interpret'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit7.passage.p005', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
“variety“ the way nutritionists intend. This problem is highlighted by new research conducted'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit7.passage.p006', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
by the American Heart Association. Researchers reviewed all the evidence published related to'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit7.passage.p007', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
dietary diversity and saw a correlation between dietary diversity and a greater intake of both'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit7.passage.p008', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
healthy and unhealthy foods. This had implications for obesity, as researchers found a greater'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit7.passage.p009', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
prevalence of obesity amongst people with a greater dietary diversity.'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit7.passage.p010', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
One author of the new study explained that their findings contradict standard dietary advice,'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit7.passage.p011', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
as most dietary guidelines around the world include a statement of eating a variety of foods. But'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit7.passage.p012', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
this advice does not seem to be supported by science, possibly because there is little agreement'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit7.passage.p013', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
about the meaning of "dietary diversity, which is not clearly and consistently defined. Some'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit7.passage.p014', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
experts measure dietary diversity by counting the number of food groups eaten, while others'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit7.passage.p015', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
look at the distribution of calories across individual foods,and still others measure how different'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit7.passage.p016', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
the foods eaten are from each other.'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit7.passage.p017', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
Although the findings of this new study contradict standard dietary advice, they do not'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit7.passage.p018', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
come as a surprise to all of the researchers involved. Dr. Rao, one of the study authors, noted'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit7.passage.p019', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
that, after 20 years of experience in the field of obesity, he has observed that people who have a'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit7.passage.p020', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
regimented lifestyle and diet tend to be thinner and healthier than people with a wide variety of'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit7.passage.p021', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
consumption. This anecdotal evidence matches the conclusions of the study, which found no'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit7.passage.p022', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
evidence that dietary diversity promotes healthy body weight or optimal eating patterns, and'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit7.passage.p023', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
limited evidence that eating a variety of foods is actually associated with consuming more'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit7.passage.p024', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
calories, poor eating patterns and weight gain. Further, there is some evidence that a greater'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit7.passage.p025', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': "
variety of food options in a single meal may delay people's feeling of fullness and actually"}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set1.unit7.passage.p026', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '

questions.prompt: It does us far more good to focus on things we can be grateful for than what makes us
options: Gratitude may be more beneficial than we commonly suppose. One recent study asked participants to write a note of thanks to someone and then estimate how surprised and happy the recipient would feel一an impact that they consistently underestimated. Another study assessed the health benefits of writing thank-you notes. The researchers found that writing as few as three weekly thank-you notes over the course of three weeks improved life satisfaction, increased happy feelings and reduced symptoms of depression.

While this research into gratitude is relatively new, the principles involved are anything but. Students of mine in a political philosophy course at Indiana University are reading Daniel Defoe5s 300-year-old Robinson Crusoe, often regarded as the first novel published in English. Left alone on an unknown island with no apparent prospect of rescue or escape, Crusoe has much to lament (悲叹).But instead of giving in to despair, he makes a list of things fbr which he is grateful, including the fact that he is the sole survivor from the shipwreck (海难)and has been able to salvage many useful items from the wreckage.

Defbe's masterpiece, which is often ranked as one of the world's greatest novels, provides a portrait of gratitude in action that is as timely and relevant today as it has ever been. It is also one with which contemporary psychology and medicine are just beginning to catch up. Simply put, for most of us, it is far more helpful to focus on the things in life fbr which we can express gratitude than those that incline us toward resentment and lamentation.

When we focus on the things we regret, such as failed relationships, family disputes, and setbacks in career and finance, we tend to become more regretful. Conversely, when we focus on the things we are grateful fbr, a greater sense of happiness tends to spread through our lives. And while no one would argue fbr cultivating a false sense of blessedness, there is mounting evidence that counting our blessings is one of the best habits we can develop to promote mental and physical health.

Gratitude has long enjoyed a privileged position in many of the world's cultural traditions. For example, some ancient Western philosophers counsel gratitude that is both enduring and complete, and some Eastern thinkers portray it as not merely an attitude but a virtue to be put into practice.

Recent scientific studies support these ancient teachings. Individuals who regularly engage in gratitude exercises, such as counting their blessings or expressing gratitude to others, exhibit increased satisfaction with relationships and fewer symptoms of physical illness. And the benefits are not only psychological and physical. They may also be moral- those who practice gratitude also view their lives less materialistically and suffer from less envy.

There are multiple explanations fbr such benefits of gratefulness. One is the fact that expressing gratitude encourages others to continue being generous, thus promoting a virtuous cycle of goodness in relationships. Similarly, grateful people may be more likely to reciprocate （回寸艮）with acts of kindness of their own. Broadly speaking, a community in which people feel grateful to one another is likely to be a more pleasant place to live than one characterized by mutual suspicion and resentment. The beneficial effects of gratitude may extend even further. For example, when many people feel good about what someone else has done for them, they experience a sense of being lifted up, with a corresponding enhancement of their regard fbr humanity. Some are inspired to attempt to become better people themselves, doing more to help bring out the best in others and bringing more goodness into the world around them.

Gratitude also tends to strengthen a sense of connection with others. W hen people want to do good things that inspire gratitude, the level of dedication in relationships tends to grow and relationships seem to last longer. And when people feel more connected, they are more likely to choose to spend their time with one another and demonstrate their feelings of affection in daily acts.

Of course, acts of kindness can also foster discomfort. For example, if people feel they are not worthy of kindness or suspect that some ulterior （另U 有用的）motive lies behind it, the benefits of gratitude will not be realized. Likewise, receiving a kindness can give rise to a sense of indebtedness, leaving beneficiaries feeling that they must now pay back whatever good they have received. Gratitude can flourish only if people are secure enough in themselves and sufficiently trusting to allow it to do so. Another obstacle to gratitude is often called a sense of entitlement. Instead of experiencing a benefaction （善行）as a good turn, people sometimes regard it as a mere payment of what they are owed, for which no one deserves any moral credit.

There are a number of practical steps anyone can take to promote a sense of gratitude. One is simply spending time on a regular basis thinking about someone who has made a difference, or perhaps writing a thank-you note or expressing such gratitude in person. Others are found in ancient religious disciplines, such as reflecting on benefactions received from another person or actually praying for the health and happiness of a benefactor. In addition to benefactions received, it is also possible to focus on opportunities to do good oneself, whether those acted on in the past or hoped for in the future. Some people are most grateftil not fbr what others have done for them but fbr chances they enjoyed to help others. In regularly reflecting on the things in his life he is grateful for, Defbe's Crusoe believes that he becomes a far better person than he would have been had he remained in the society from which he originally set out on his voyage.

Reflecting on generosity and gratitude, the great basketball coach John W ooden once offered two counsels to his players and students. First, he said, “It is impossible to have a perfect day unless you have done something for someone who will never be able to repay you.55 In saying this, W ooden sought to promote purely generous acts, as opposed to those performed with an expectation of reward. Second, he said, “Give thanks fbr your blessings every day.55

Some faith traditions incorporate such practices into the rhythm of daily life. For example, adherents of some religions offer prayers of thanksgiving every morning before rising and every night before lying down to sleep. Others offer thanks throughout the day, such as before meals. Other less frequent special events, such as births, deaths and marriages, may also be heralded by such prayers.

W hen Defoe depicted Robinson Crusoe making thanksgiving a daily part of his island life, he was anticipating findings in social science and medicine that would not appear for hundreds of years. Yet he was also reflecting the wisdom of religious and philosophical traditions that extend back thousands of years. Gratitude is one of the healthiest and most nourishing of all states of mind, and those who adopt it as a habit are enriching not only their own lives but also the lives of those around them.

options: Gratitude may be more beneficial than we commonly suppose. One recent study asked participants to write a note of thanks to someone and then estimate how surprised and happy the recipient would feel一an impact that they consistently underestimated. Another study assessed the health benefits of writing thank-you notes. The researchers found that writing as few as three weekly thank-you notes over the course of three weeks improved life satisfaction, increased happy feelings and reduced symptoms of depression.

While this research into gratitude is relatively new, the principles involved are anything but. Students of mine in a political philosophy course at Indiana University are reading Daniel Defoe5s 300-year-old Robinson Crusoe, often regarded as the first novel published in English. Left alone on an unknown island with no apparent prospect of rescue or escape, Crusoe has much to lament (悲叹).But instead of giving in to despair, he makes a list of things fbr which he is grateful, including the fact that he is the sole survivor from the shipwreck (海难)and has been able to salvage many useful items from the wreckage.

Defbe's masterpiece, which is often ranked as one of the world's greatest novels, provides a portrait of gratitude in action that is as timely and relevant today as it has ever been. It is also one with which contemporary psychology and medicine are just beginning to catch up. Simply put, for most of us, it is far more helpful to focus on the things in life fbr which we can express gratitude than those that incline us toward resentment and lamentation.

When we focus on the things we regret, such as failed relationships, family disputes, and setbacks in career and finance, we tend to become more regretful. Conversely, when we focus on the things we are grateful fbr, a greater sense of happiness tends to spread through our lives. And while no one would argue fbr cultivating a false sense of blessedness, there is mounting evidence that counting our blessings is one of the best habits we can develop to promote mental and physical health.

Gratitude has long enjoyed a privileged position in many of the world's cultural traditions. For example, some ancient Western philosophers counsel gratitude that is both enduring and complete, and some Eastern thinkers portray it as not merely an attitude but a virtue to be put into practice.

Recent scientific studies support these ancient teachings. Individuals who regularly engage in gratitude exercises, such as counting their blessings or expressing gratitude to others, exhibit increased satisfaction with relationships and fewer symptoms of physical illness. And the benefits are not only psychological and physical. They may also be moral- those who practice gratitude also view their lives less materialistically and suffer from less envy.

There are multiple explanations fbr such benefits of gratefulness. One is the fact that expressing gratitude encourages others to continue being generous, thus promoting a virtuous cycle of goodness in relationships. Similarly, grateful people may be more likely to reciprocate （回寸艮）with acts of kindness of their own. Broadly speaking, a community in which people feel grateful to one another is likely to be a more pleasant place to live than one characterized by mutual suspicion and resentment. The beneficial effects of gratitude may extend even further. For example, when many people feel good about what someone else has done for them, they experience a sense of being lifted up, with a corresponding enhancement of their regard fbr humanity. Some are inspired to attempt to become better people themselves, doing more to help bring out the best in others and bringing more goodness into the world around them.

Gratitude also tends to strengthen a sense of connection with others. W hen people want to do good things that inspire gratitude, the level of dedication in relationships tends to grow and relationships seem to last longer. And when people feel more connected, they are more likely to choose to spend their time with one another and demonstrate their feelings of affection in daily acts.

Of course, acts of kindness can also foster discomfort. For example, if people feel they are not worthy of kindness or suspect that some ulterior （另U 有用的）motive lies behind it, the benefits of gratitude will not be realized. Likewise, receiving a kindness can give rise to a sense of indebtedness, leaving beneficiaries feeling that they must now pay back whatever good they have received. Gratitude can flourish only if people are secure enough in themselves and sufficiently trusting to allow it to do so. Another obstacle to gratitude is often called a sense of entitlement. Instead of experiencing a benefaction （善行）as a good turn, people sometimes regard it as a mere payment of what they are owed, for which no one deserves any moral credit.

There are a number of practical steps anyone can take to promote a sense of gratitude. One is simply spending time on a regular basis thinking about someone who has made a difference, or perhaps writing a thank-you note or expressing such gratitude in person. Others are found in ancient religious disciplines, such as reflecting on benefactions received from another person or actually praying for the health and happiness of a benefactor. In addition to benefactions received, it is also possible to focus on opportunities to do good oneself, whether those acted on in the past or hoped for in the future. Some people are most grateftil not fbr what others have done for them but fbr chances they enjoyed to help others. In regularly reflecting on the things in his life he is grateful for, Defbe's Crusoe believes that he becomes a far better person than he would have been had he remained in the society from which he originally set out on his voyage.

Reflecting on generosity and gratitude, the great basketball coach John W ooden once offered two counsels to his players and students. First, he said, “It is impossible to have a perfect day unless you have done something for someone who will never be able to repay you.55 In saying this, W ooden sought to promote purely generous acts, as opposed to those performed with an expectation of reward. Second, he said, “Give thanks fbr your blessings every day.55

Some faith traditions incorporate such practices into the rhythm of daily life. For example, adherents of some religions offer prayers of thanksgiving every morning before rising and every night before lying down to sleep. Others offer thanks throughout the day, such as before meals. Other less frequent special events, such as births, deaths and marriages, may also be heralded by such prayers.

W hen Defoe depicted Robinson Crusoe making thanksgiving a daily part of his island life, he was anticipating findings in social science and medicine that would not appear for hundreds of years. Yet he was also reflecting the wisdom of religious and philosophical traditions that extend back thousands of years. Gratitude is one of the healthiest and most nourishing of all states of mind, and those who adopt it as a habit are enriching not only their own lives but also the lives of those around them.

Technological innovations'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:06:set1.unit6.passage.p002', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': 'reshape people as they use these innovations to control their environment. Artificial'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:06:set1.unit6.passage.p003', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
intelligence, fbr example, is altering humanity.'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:06:set1.unit6.passage.p004', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
While the term AI conjures up anxieties about killer robots or catastrophic levels of'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:06:set1.unit6.passage.p005', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
unemployment, there are other, deeper implications. As AI increasingly shapes the human'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:06:set1.unit6.passage.p006', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
experience, how does this change what it means to be human? Central to the problem is a'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:06:set1.unit6.passage.p007', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': "
person's capacity to make choices, particularly judgments that have moral implications."}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:06:set1.unit6.passage.p008', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
Aristotle argued that the capacity for making practical judgments depends on regularly'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:06:set1.unit6.passage.p009', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
making them——on habit and practice. We see the emergence of machines as substitute'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:06:set1.unit6.passage.p010', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
judges in a variety of everyday contexts as a potential threat to people learning how to'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:06:set1.unit6.passage.p011', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
effectively exercise judgment themselves.'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:06:set1.unit6.passage.p012', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
In the workplace, managers routinely make decisions about whom to hire or fire and which loan to approve, to name a few. These are areas where algorithmic (算法的)'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:06:set1.unit6.passage.p013', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
prescription is replacing human judgment, and so people who might have had the chance to'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:06:set1.unit6.passage.p014', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
develop practical judgment in these areas no longer will.'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:06:set1.unit6.passage.p015', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': "
Recommendation engines, which are increasingly prevalent intermediaries in people's"}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:06:set1.unit6.passage.p016', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
consumption of culture, may serve to constrain choice and minimize luck. By presenting'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:06:set1.unit6.passage.p017', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
consumers with algorithmically selected choices of what to watch, read, stream and visit'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:06:set1.unit6.passage.p018', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
next, companies are replacing human taste with machine taste. In one sense, this is helpful.'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:06:set1.unit6.passage.p019', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
After all, machines can survey a wider range of choices than any individual is likely to have'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:06:set1.unit6.passage.p020', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
the time or energy to do on their own.'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:06:set1.unit6.passage.p021', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
At the same time, though,this selection is optimizing fbr what people are likely to'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:06:set1.unit6.passage.p022', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': "
prefer based on what they've preferred in the past. We think there is some risk that people's"}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:06:set1.unit6.passage.p023', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
options will be constrained by their past in a new and unanticipated way.'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:06:set1.unit6.passage.p024', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
As machine learning algorithms improve and as they train on more extensive data sets,'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:06:set1.unit6.passage.p025', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
larger parts of everyday life are likely to become utterly predictable. The predictions are'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:06:set1.unit6.passage.p026', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
going to get better and better, and they will ultimately make common experiences more'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:06:set1.unit6.passage.p027', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
efficient and pleasant.'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:06:set1.unit6.passage.p028', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': "
Algorithms could soon-if they don't already—have a better idea about which show"}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:06:set1.unit6.passage.p029', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': "
you'd like to watch next and which job candidate you should hire than you do. One day,"}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:06:set1.unit6.passage.p030', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
humans may even find a way for machines to make these decisions without some of the'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:06:set1.unit6.passage.p031', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
biases that humans typically display.'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:06:set1.unit6.passage.p032', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
But to the extent that unpredictability is part of how people understand themselves and'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:06:set1.unit6.passage.p033', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
part of what people like about themselves, humanity is in the process of losing something'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:06:set1.unit6.passage.p034', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
significant. As they become more and more predictable, the creatures inhabiting the'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:06:set1.unit6.passage.p035', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
increasingly Ai-mediated world will become less and less like us.'}]}

questions.prompt: What do we learn about the deeper implications of AI?
options: It is causing catastrophic levels of unemployment.
It is doing physical harm to human operators.
questions.answer: It is reshaping humanity.

questions.prompt: What is the consequence of algorithmic prescription replacing human judgment?
options: People lose the chance to cultivate the ability to make practical judgments.
People are prevented from participating in making major decisions in the workplace.
Managers no longer have the chance to decide which loan to approve.
Managers do not need to take the trouble to determine who to hire or fire.
questions.answer: People lose the chance to cultivate the ability to make practical judgments.

questions.prompt: What may result from increasing application of recommendation engines in our
options: Consumers will have much limited choice.
Consumers will actually enjoy better luck.
It will be easier to decide on what to enjoy.
Humans will develop tastes similar to machines5.
questions.answer: Consumers will have much limited choice.

questions.prompt: What is likely to happen to larger parts of our daily life as machine learning algorithms
options: They will turn out to be more pleasant.
They will repeat our past experience.
They may become better and better.
questions.answer: They can be completely anticipated.

questions.prompt: Why does the author say the creatures living in the more and more Ai-mediated world
options: They will have lost the most significant human element of being intelligent.
They will no longer possess the human characteristic of being unpredictable.
They will not be able to understand themselves as we can do today.
They will be deprived of what their predecessors were proud of about themselves.
questions.answer: They will no longer possess the human characteristic of being unpredictable.

reading.passage: {'blocks': [{'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit5.passage.p001', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '[A] The fog still chills the morning air and the cable cars still climb halfway to the stars. Yet on the ground, the Bay area has changed greatly since singer Tony Bennett left his heart here. Silicon Valley and the tech industry have led the region into a period of unprecedented wealth and innovation. But existing political and land limits have caused an alarming housing crisis and astronomical rise in social and economic difference.'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit5.passage.p002', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '[B] While the residents of most cities display pride and support for their home industries, drastic market distortions in the San Francisco Bay Area have created boiling resentment in the region towards the tech industry. A vocal minority is even calling on officials to punish those who are benefitting from the economic and housing boom. If this boom and its consequences are not resolved, a drastic increase in social and economic difference may have a profound impact on the region for generations. A history and analysis of this transformation may hold invaluable insights about the opportunities. Perils of tech cities are currently being cultivated across the US, and indeed around the world.'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit5.passage.p003', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': "[C] According to a recent study, San Francisco ranks first in California for economic difference. The average income of the top 1% of households in the city averages $3.6 million. This is 44 times the average income of those at the bottom, which stands at $81,094. The top 1% of the San Francisco peninsula's share of total income now extends to 30.8% of the region's income. This was a dramatic jump from 1989, where it stood at 15.8%."}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit5.passage.p004', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': "[D] The region's economy has been fundamentally transformed by the technology industry springing from Silicon Valley. Policies pushed by Mayor Ed Lee provided tax breaks for tech companies to set up shop along the city's long-neglected Mid-Market area. The city is now home to Twitter, Uber, Airbnb, Pinterest, Dropbox and others. In short, the Bay Area has become a global magnet for those with specialized skills, which has in turn helped fuel economic enthusiasm, and this economic growth has reduced unemployment to 3.4%, an admirable feat."}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit5.passage.p005', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '[E] In spite of all that, the strength of the recent job growth, combined with policies that have traditionally limited housing development in the city and throughout the peninsula, did not help ease the affordability crisis. In 2015 alone, the Bay Area added 64,000 in jobs. In the same year, only 5,000 new homes were built.'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit5.passage.p006', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '[F] With the average house in the city costing over $1.25 million and average flat prices over $1.11 million, the minimum qualifying income to purchase a house has increased to $254,000. Considering that the average household income in the city currently stands at around $80,000, it is not an exaggeration to say that the dream of home ownership is now beyond the grasp of the vast majority of today’s people who rent.'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit5.passage.p007', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '[G] For generations, the stability and prosperity of the American middle class has been anchored by home ownership. Studies have consistently shown that the value of land has overtaken overall income growth, thus providing a huge advantage to property owners as a vehicle of wealth building. When home prices soar above the reach of most households, the gap between the rich and the poor dramatically increases.'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit5.passage.p008', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '[H] If contributing factors leading to housing becoming less than affordable are not resolved over multiple generations, a small elite will control a vast share of the country’s total wealth. The result? A society where the threat of class warfare would loom large. A society’s level of happiness is tied less to measures of quantitative wealth and more to measures of qualitative wealth. This means that how a person judges their security in comparison to their neighbors’ has more of an impact on their happiness than their objective standard of living. At the same time, when a system no longer provides opportunities for the majority to participate in wealth building, it not only robs those who are excluded from opportunities, but also deprives them of their dignity.'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit5.passage.p009', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '[I] San Francisco and the Bay Area have long been committed to values which embrace inclusion and rejection of mainstream culture. To see these values coming apart so publicly adds insult to injury for a region once defined by its progressive social fabric. In the face of resentment, it is human to want revenge. But deteriorating policies such as heavily taxing technology companies or real estate developers are not likely to shift the balance.'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit5.passage.p010', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '[J] The housing crisis is caused by two primary factors: the growing desirability of the Bay Area as a place to live due to its excellent economy, and our limited housing stock. Although the city is experiencing an unprecedented boom in new housing, more units are sorely needed. Protection policies were originally designed to suppress bad development and boost historic preservation in our urban areas. Now, too many developers are experiencing excessive delays. Meanwhile, there are the land limitations of the Bay Area to consider. The region is surrounded by water and mountains. Local governments need to aid development as well. This means increasing housing density throughout the region and building upwards while streamlining the approval process.'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit5.passage.p011', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '[K] Real estate alone will not solve the problem, of course. Transportation, too, needs to be updated and infrastructure extended to link distant regions to Silicon Valley and the city. We need to build an effective high-speed commuting system linking the high-priced and crowded Bay Area with the low-priced and low-density Central Valley. This would dramatically reduce travel times. And based on the operating speeds of hovering trains used in countries such as Japan or Spain, high-speed rail could shorten the time to travel between San Francisco and California’s capital, Sacramento, or from Stockton to San Jose, to under 30 minutes. This system would bring once distant regions within reasonable commute to heavy job centers. The city also needs to update existing transportation routes combined with smart home-building policies that dramatically increase housing density in areas surrounding high-speed rail stations. By doing so, we will be able to build affordable housing within acceptable commuting distances for a significant bulk of the workforce.'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit5.passage.p012', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '[L] Our threatening housing crisis forces the difficult question of what type of society we would like to be. Will it be one where the elite command the vast bulk of wealth and regional culture is defined by an aggressive business world? We were recently treated to a taste of the latter, when local tech employee Justin Keller wrote an open letter to the city complaining about having to see homeless people on his way to work.'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit5.passage.p013', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': "[M] It doesn't have to be this way. But solutions need to be implemented now, before angry crowds grow from a nuisance to serious concern. It may take less than you might think. And in fact, the solutions to our housing crisis are already fairly clear. We need to increase the density of housing units. We need to use existing technology to shorten travel times and break the land limits. There is a way to solve complex social and economic problems without abandoning social responsibility. This is the Bay Area's opportunity to prove that it can innovate more than just technology."}]}

The city is now hom e to Tw itter, U ber, A irbnb, Pinterest, D ropbox and others. In short, the Bay A rea has becom e a global m agnet for those w ith specialized skills, w hich has in turn helped fuel econom ic enthusiasm , and this econom ic grow th has reduced unem ploym ent to 3.4%, an adm irable feat.

In spite of all that, the strength of the recent job grow th, com bined w ith policies that have traditionally lim ited housing developm ent in the city and throughout the peninsula, did not help ease the affordability crisis. In 2015 alone, the Bay A rea added 64,000 in jobs. In the sam e year, only 5,000 new hom es w ere built.

W ith the average house in the city costing over $1.25 m illion and average flat prices over $1.11 m illion, the m inim um qualifying incom e to purchase a house has increased to $254,000.Considering that the average household incom e in the city currently stands at around $80,000, it is not an exaggeration to say that the dream of hom e ow nership is now beyond the grasp of the vast m ajority of today9s people w ho rent.

For generations, the stability and prosperity of the A m erican m iddle class has been anchored by hom e ow nership. Studies have consistently show n that the value of land has overtaken overall incom e grow th, thus providing a huge advantage to property ow ners as a vehicle of w ealth building. W hen hom e prices soar above the reach of m ost households, the gap betw een the rich and the poor dram atically increases.

If contributing factors leading to housing becom ing less than affordable are not resolved over m ultiple generations, a sm all elite w ill control a vast share of the country,s total w ealth. The result? A society w here the threat of class w arfare w ould loom large. A society 9s level of happiness is tied less to m easures of quantitative w ealth and m ore to m easures of qualitative w ealth. This m eans that how a person judges their security in com parison to their neighbors? has m ore of an im pact on their happiness than their objective standard of living. A t the sam e tim e, w hen a system no longer provides opportunities for the m ajority to participate in w ealth building, it not only robs those w ho are excluded from opportunities, but also deprives them of their dignity.

San Francisco and the Bay A rea have long been com m itted to values w hich em brace inclusion and rejection of m ainstream culture.To see these values com ing apart so publicly adds insult to injury for a region once defined by its progressive social fabric. In the face of resentm ent, it is hum an to w ant revenge.But deteriorating policies such as heavily taxing technology com panies or real estate developers are not likely to shift the balance.

The housing crisis is caused by tw o prim ary factors: the grow ing desirability of the Bay A rea as a place to live due to its excellent econom y, and our lim ited housing stock. A lthough the city is experiencing an unprecedented boom in new housing, m ore units are sorely needed.Protection policies w ere originally designed to suppress bad developm ent and boost historic preservation in our urban areas. N ow , too m any developers are experiencing excessive delays.M eanw hile, there are the land lim itations of the Bay A rea to consider. The region is surrounded by w ater and m ountains. Local governm ents need to aid developm ent as w ell. This m eans increasing housing density throughout the region and building upw ards w hile stream lining the approval process.

R eal estate alone w ill not solve the problem , of course. Transportation, too, needs to be updated and infrastructure extended to link distant regions to Silicon V alley and the city. W e need to build an effective high-speed com m uting system linking the high-priced and crow ded Bay A rea w ith the low -priced and low -density Central V alley. This w ould dram atically reduce travel tim es. A nd based on the operating speeds of hovering trains used in countries such as Japan or Spain, high-speed rail could shorten the tim e to travel betw een San Francisco and California^ capital, Sacram ento, or from Stockton to San Jose, to under 30 m inutes. This system w ould bring once distant regions w ithin reasonable com m ute to heavy job centers. The city also needs to update existing transportation routes com bined w ith sm art hom e-building policies that dram atically increase housing density in areas surrounding high-speed rail stations. By doing so, w e w ill be able to build affordable housing w ithin acceptable com m uting distances for a significant bulk of the w orkforce.

O ur threatening housing crisis forces the difficult question of w hat type of society w e w ould like to be. W ill it be one w here the elite com m and the vast bulk of w ealth and regional culture is defined by an aggressive business w orld? W e w ere recently treated to a taste of the latter, w hen local tech em ployee Justin K eller w rote an open letter to the city com plaining about having to see hom eless people on his w ay to w ork.

It doesn't have to be this w ay. But solutions need to be im plem ented now , before angry crow ds grow from a nuisance to serious concern. It m ay take less than you m ight think. A nd in fact, the solutions to our housing crisis are already fairly clear. W e need to increase the density of housing units. W e need to use existing technology to shorten travel tim es and break the land lim its. There is a w ay to solve com plex social and econom ic problem s w ithout abandoning social responsibility. This is the Bay A rea's opportunity to prove that it can innovate m ore than just technology.

{'blocks': [{'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit6.passage.p001', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': 'The ability to make inferences from same and different, once thought to be unique to'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit6.passage.p002', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': 'humans, is viewed as a cornerstone of abstract intelligent thought. A new study, however, has'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit6.passage.p003', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
shown that what psychologists call same-different discrimination is present in creatures'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit6.passage.p004', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
generally seen as unintelligent: newborn ducklings (小鸭) .'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit6.passage.p005', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
The study, published Thursday in Science, challenges our idea of what it means to have a'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit6.passage.p006', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
birdbrain, said Edward Wasserman, an experimental psychologist at the University of Iowa who'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit6.passage.p007', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
wrote an independent review of the study.'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit6.passage.p008', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
“In fact, birds are extremely intelligent and our problem pretty much lies in figuring out'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit6.passage.p009', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': "
how to get them to 'talk' to us, or tell us how smart they really are,“ he said."}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit6.passage.p010', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
Antone Martinho and Alex Kacelnik, co-authors of the new paper, devised a clever'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit6.passage.p011', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
experiment to better test bird intelligence.'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit6.passage.p012', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
First, they took 1-day-old ducklings and exposed them to a pair of moving objects. The two'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit6.passage.p013', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
objects were either the same or different in shape or color. Then they exposed each duckling to'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit6.passage.p014', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
two entirely new pairs of moving objects.'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit6.passage.p015', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
The researchers found that about 70% of the ducklings preferred to move toward the pair of'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit6.passage.p016', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
objects that had the same shape or color relationship as the first objects they saw. A duckling'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit6.passage.p017', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
that was first shown two green spheres, in other words, was more likely to move toward a pair'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit6.passage.p018', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
of blue spheres than a mismatched pair of orange and purple spheres.'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit6.passage.p019', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': "
Ducklings go through a rapid learning process called imprinting shortly after birth一it's"}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit6.passage.p020', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
what allows them to identify and follow their mothers.'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit6.passage.p021', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
These findings suggest that ducklings use abstract relationships between sensory inputs like color, shape, sounds and odor to recognize their mothers, said Dr. Kacelnik.'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit6.passage.p022', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
By studying imprinting, the authors of this study have shown for the first time that an'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit6.passage.p023', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
animal can learn relationships between concepts without training, said Jeffrey Katz, an'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit6.passage.p024', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
experimental psychologist at Auburn University who was not involved in the study.'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit6.passage.p025', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
Previous studies have suggested that other animals, including pigeons, dolphins, honeybees'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit6.passage.p026', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
and some primates (灵长类动物)， can discern same from different, but only after extensive'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit6.passage.p027', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
training.'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit6.passage.p028', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
Adding ducklings to the list-particularly untrained newborn ducklings一suggests that the'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit6.passage.p029', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
ability to compare abstract concepts “is far more necessary to a wider variety of animals5'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit6.passage.p030', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
survival than we previously thought, Dr. Martinho said.He believes the ability is so crucial'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit6.passage.p031', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
because it helps animals consider context when identifying objects in their environment.'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit6.passage.p032', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
It's clear from this study and others like it that "animals process and appreciate far more of'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit6.passage.p033', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
the intricacies in their world than we've ever understood, Dr. Wasserman said. "We are in a'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit6.passage.p034', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
revolutionary phase in terms of our ability to understand the minds of other animals.^^'}]}

{'blocks': [{'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit7.passage.p001', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': 'The suggestion that people should aim for dietary diversity by trying to eat a variety of'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit7.passage.p002', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': 'foods has been a basic public health recommendation for decades in the United States and'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit7.passage.p003', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
elsewhere. Now, however, experts are warning that aiming for a diverse diet may actually lead'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit7.passage.p004', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
to just eating more calories, and, thus, to obesity. One issue is that people may not interpret'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit7.passage.p005', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
“variety“ the way nutritionists intend. This problem is highlighted by new research conducted'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit7.passage.p006', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
by the American Heart Association. Researchers reviewed all the evidence published related to'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit7.passage.p007', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
dietary diversity and saw a correlation between dietary diversity and a greater intake of both'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit7.passage.p008', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
healthy and unhealthy foods. This had implications for obesity, as researchers found a greater'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit7.passage.p009', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
prevalence of obesity amongst people with a greater dietary diversity.'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit7.passage.p010', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
One author of the new study explained that their findings contradict standard dietary advice,'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit7.passage.p011', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
as most dietary guidelines around the world include a statement of eating a variety of foods. But'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit7.passage.p012', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
this advice does not seem to be supported by science, possibly because there is little agreement'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit7.passage.p013', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
about the meaning of "dietary diversity, which is not clearly and consistently defined. Some'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit7.passage.p014', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
experts measure dietary diversity by counting the number of food groups eaten, while others'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit7.passage.p015', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
look at the distribution of calories across individual foods,and still others measure how different'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit7.passage.p016', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
the foods eaten are from each other.'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit7.passage.p017', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
Although the findings of this new study contradict standard dietary advice, they do not'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit7.passage.p018', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
come as a surprise to all of the researchers involved. Dr. Rao, one of the study authors, noted'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit7.passage.p019', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
that, after 20 years of experience in the field of obesity, he has observed that people who have a'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit7.passage.p020', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
regimented lifestyle and diet tend to be thinner and healthier than people with a wide variety of'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit7.passage.p021', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
consumption. This anecdotal evidence matches the conclusions of the study, which found no'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit7.passage.p022', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
evidence that dietary diversity promotes healthy body weight or optimal eating patterns, and'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit7.passage.p023', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
limited evidence that eating a variety of foods is actually associated with consuming more'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit7.passage.p024', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
calories, poor eating patterns and weight gain. Further, there is some evidence that a greater'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit7.passage.p025', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': "
variety of food options in a single meal may delay people's feeling of fullness and actually"}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit7.passage.p026', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
increase how much they eat.'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit7.passage.p027', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
Based on their findings, the researchers endorse a diet consisting of a limited number of'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit7.passage.p028', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
healthy foods such as vegetables, fruits, grains, and poultry. They also recommend that people'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit7.passage.p029', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
simultaneously endeavor to restrict consumption of sweets, sugar and red meat. The researchers'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit7.passage.p030', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
stress, however, that their dietary recommendations do not imply dietary diversity is never'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit7.passage.p031', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
positive, and that, in the past, diversity in diets of whole, unprocessed food may have actually'}, {'blockKey': 'cet6:2023:03:set2.unit7.passage.p032', 'type': 'paragraph', 'text': '
been very beneficial.'}]}

questions.prompt: Socially prescribed perfectionism is described as one's self-esteem depending on other
options: When psychologist Jessica Pryor lived near an internationally renowned university, she once saw a student walking into a library holding a sleeping bag and a coffee maker. She has heard of graduate students spending 12 to 18 hours at a time in the lab. Their schedules are meant to be literally punishing: If they are scientists-in-training, they won't allow themselves to watch Netflix until their experiments start generating results. ""Relationships become estranged (疏远的)——people stop inviting them to social gatherings or dinner parties, which leads them to spend even more time in the lab/5 Pryor told me.

Along with other therapists, Pryor, who is now with the Family Institute at Northwestern University, is trying to sound the alarm about a tendency among young adults and college students to strive for perfection in their work- sometimes at any cost. Though it is often portrayed as a positive trait, Pryor and others say extreme perfectionism can lead to depression, anxiety, and even suicide.

What's more, perfectionism seems to be on the rise. In a study of thousands of American, Canadian, and British college students published earlier this year, Thomas Curran of the University of Bath and Andrew Hill of York St. John University found that today 5s college students report higher levels of perfectionism than college students did during the 1990s or early 2000s. They measured three types of perfectionism: self-oriented, or a desire to be perfect; socially prescribed, or a desire to live up to others5 expectations; and other-oriented, or holding others to unrealistic standards. From 1989 to 2016, they found, self-oriented perfectionism scores increased by 10 percent, socially prescribed scores rose by 33 percent, and other-oriented perfectionism increased by 16 percent.

A person living with an other-oriented perfectionist might feel criticized by the perfectionist spouse for not doing household chores exactly the "right" way. "One of the most common things couples argue about is the proper way of loading the dishwasher；' says Amy Bach, a psychologist in Providence, Rhode Island.

Curran describes socially prescribed perfectionism as "My self-esteem is contingent on what other people think " His study didn't examine the causal reasons for its rise, but he assumes that the rise of both standardized testing and social media might play a role. These days, Linkedln alerts us when our rival gets a new job, and Instagram can let us know how well "liked“ our lives are compared with a friend5s. In an opinion piece earlier this year, Curran and Hill argue that society has also become more dog-eat-dog. "Over the last 50 years, public interest and civic responsibility have been progressively eroded,“ they write, "replaced by a focus on self-interest and competition in a supposedly free and open marketplace.W e strive for perfection, it seems, because we feel we must in order to get ahead. Michael Brustein, a clinical psychologist in Manhattan, says when he first began practicing in 2007, he was surprised by how prevalent perfectionism was among his clients, despite how little his graduate training had focused on the phenomenon. He sees perfectionism in, among others, clients who are entrepreneurs, artists, and tech employees. "You're in New York because you're ambitious, you have this need to strive/5 he says. "But then your whole identity gets wrapped into a goal”

Perfectionism can, of course, be a positive force. Think of professional athletes, who train aggressively for ever-higher levels of competition. In well-adjusted perfectionism, someone who doesn't get the gold is able to forget the setback and move on. In maladaptive (不 当的)perfectionism, meanwhile, people make an archive of all their failures. They revisit these archives constantly, thinking, as Pryor puts it, “I need to make myself feel terrible so I don5t do this again.5, Then they double down, "raising the expectation bar even higher, which increases the likelihood of defeat, which makes you self-critical, so you raise the bar higher, work even harder,55 she says. Next comes failure, shame, and pushing yourself even harder toward even higher and more impossible goals. Meeting them becomes an "all or nothing“ premise. Pryor offered this example: "Even if Tm an incredible attorney, if I don't make partner in the same pacing as one of my colleagues, clearly that means I'm a failure/5

Brustein says his perfectionist clients tend to devalue their accomplishments, so that every time a goal is achieved, the high lasts only a short time, like “a gas tank with a hole in it.55 If the boss says you did a great job, it's because he doesn't know anything. If the audience likes your work, that's because it's too stupid to know what good art actually is. But, therapists say, there are also different ways perfectionism manifests. Some perfectionists are always pushing themselves forward. But others actually fall behind on work, unable to complete assignments unless they are, well, perfect. Or they might handicap their performance ahead of time. They5re the ones partying until 2 a. m. the night before the final, so that when the grade C rolls in, there5s a ready excuse.

While educators and parents have successfully convinced students of the need to be high performing and diligent, the experts told me, they haven't adequately prepared them for the inevitability of failure. Instead of praises like "You're so smart,55 parents and educators should say things like "You really stuck with it；' Pryor says, to emphasize the value of perseverance over intrinsic talent. Pryor notes that many of her clients are wary shell "turn them into some degenerate couch potato and teach them to be okay with it" Instead, she tries to help them think through the parts of their perfectionism they5d like to keep, and to lose the parts that are ruining their lives.

Bach, who sees many students from Brown University, says some of them don't even go out on weekends, let alone weekdays. She tells them, “Aim high, but get comfortable with good enough.55 When they don't get some award, she encourages them to remember that “one outcome is not a basis for a broad conclusion about the person's intelligence, qualifications, or potential fbr the future.55

The treatment for perfectionism might be as simple as having patients keep logs of things they can be proud of, or having them behave imperfectly in small ways, just to see how it feels. ccWe might have them hang the towels crooked (不正的)or wear some clothing inside out；' says Martin Antony, a professor in the department of psychology at Ryerson University in Toronto.

Brustein likes to get his perfectionist clients to create values that are important to them, then try to shift their focus to living according to those values rather than achieving specific goals. It's a play on the "You really stuck with it“ message fbr kids. In other words, it isn5t about doing a headstand in yoga class; it's about going to yoga class in the first place, because you like to be the kind of person who takes care of herself. But he warns that some people go into therapy expecting too much- an instant transformation of themselves from a pathological (病 态的)perfectionist to a (still high-achieving) non-perfectionist. They try to be perfect, in other words, at no longer being perfect.

increasing commercialization of education is eroding many children's self-esteem.
the growing desire fbr wealth is contributing to a rising rate of depression.
the craving for purchasing material things is nurtured throughout one's life.
questions.answer: life-long consumerism is causing more and more cases of psychological problems.

questions.prompt: W hat does the author imply about the impact of advertising?

questions.prompt: Why are many people opposed to monitoring employee performance?

It is universally deemed anti-human by nature.
It does both mental and physical harm to employees monitored.
It enables firms to squeeze maximal productivity from employees.
questions.answer: It puts workers under constant pressure.

It can alert employees to intrusion into their privacy.
It can protect employees against aggressive behavior.
